claim: Cerebral blood flow is highly sensitive to changes in CO2/H+ where an increase in CO2/H+ causes vasodilation and increased blood flow.
source: Cerebral blood flow is highly sensitive to changes in CO2/H+ where an increase in CO2/H+ causes vasodilation and increased blood flow.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, and is supported by citations in the introduction (Ainslie and Duffin, 2009).

claim: Tissue CO2/H+ functions as the main stimulus for breathing by activating chemosensitive neurons that control respiratory output.
source: Tissue CO2/H+ also functions as the main stimulus for breathing by activating chemosensitive neurons that control respiratory output.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015).

claim: Purinergic signaling, possibly through P2Y2/4 receptors, in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) maintains arteriole tone during high CO2/H+.
source: Here, we show in rat that purinergic signaling, possibly through P2Y2/4 receptors, in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) maintains arteriole tone during high CO2/H+ and disruption of this mechanism decreases the CO2ventilatory response.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Disruption of purinergic signaling in the RTN decreases the CO2 ventilatory response.
source: Here, we show in rat that purinergic signaling, possibly through P2Y2/4 receptors, in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) maintains arteriole tone during high CO2/H+ and disruption of this mechanism decreases the CO2ventilatory response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: CO2/H+-dependent regulation of vascular tone in the RTN is opposite to the rest of the cerebral vascular tree.
source: Our discovery that CO2/H+-dependent regulation of vascular tone in the RTN is the opposite to the rest of the cerebral vascular tree is novel and fundamentally important for understanding how regulation of vascular tone is tailored to support neural function and behavior, in this case the drive to breathe.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing RTN and cortical arterioles in Figures 1-3 and 5.

claim: A modest alkalosis of just 0.2 pH units can trigger seizure activity.
source: For example, a modest alkalosis of just 0.2 pH units can trigger seizure activity; conversely, a similar degree of acidification can inhibit cortical activity (Schuchmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schuchmann et al., 2006.

claim: A similar degree of acidification (0.2 pH units) can inhibit cortical activity.
source: For example, a modest alkalosis of just 0.2 pH units can trigger seizure activity; conversely, a similar degree of acidification can inhibit cortical activity (Schuchmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schuchmann et al., 2006.

claim: The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is a region critical for respiratory chemoreception.
source: The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is a region critical for respiratory chemoreception (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation to Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015.

claim: The RTN contains a subset of neurons that are intrinsically sensitive to changes in CO2/H+.
source: This region contains a subset of neurons that are intrinsically sensitive to changes in CO2/H+ (Mulkey et al., 2004: Wang et al., 2013) and relay responses to further respiratory control regions, such as the ventral respiratory complex to control breathing rate, inspiratory amplitude, active expiration and airway patency (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mulkey et al., 2004 and Wang et al., 2013.

claim: RTN neurons relay responses to respiratory control regions such as the ventral respiratory complex to control breathing rate, inspiratory amplitude, active expiration and airway patency.
source: This region contains a subset of neurons that are intrinsically sensitive to changes in CO2/H+ (Mulkey et al., 2004: Wang et al., 2013) and relay responses to further respiratory control regions, such as the ventral respiratory complex to control breathing rate, inspiratory amplitude, active expiration and airway patency (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Silva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015 and Silva et al., 2016.

claim: Disrupting mechanisms by which RTN neurons sense CO2/H+ abolishes ventilatory responses to CO2 and results in severe apnea.
source: Disrupting mechanisms by which RTN neurons sense CO2/H+ abolishes ventilatory responses to CO2 and results in severe apnea (Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2015.

claim: RTN astrocytes support chemoreception by providing a CO2/H+-dependent purinergic drive that enhances activity of chemosensitive neurons.
source: Interestingly, RTN astrocytes also support chemoreception by providing a CO2/H+-dependent purinergic drive that enhances activity of chemosensitive neurons (Gourine et al., 2010; Wenker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gourine et al., 2010 and Wenker et al., 2012.

claim: The function of RTN astrocytes in chemoreception is unique to the RTN since astrocytes elsewhere do not respond similarly to changes in pH.
source: This function of RTN astrocytes is unique to the RTN since astrocytes elsewhere do not respond similarly to changes in pH (Gourine et al., 2010; Sobrinho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gourine et al., 2010 and Sobrinho et al., 2014.

claim: Vascular CO2 reactivity has been assumed to be a common feature of the entire cerebrovascular tree for more than a century.
source: For more than a century, vascular CO2 reactivity has been assumed to be a common feature of the entire cerebrovascular tree (Ainslie and Duffin, 2009; Roy and Sherrington, 1890).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ainslie and Duffin, 2009 and Roy and Sherrington, 1890.

claim: If CO2/H+-induced vasodilation were to occur in chemosensitive regions it would accelerate removal of tissue CO2/H+ and effectively counter-regulate activity of respiratory chemoreceptors.
source: However, if CO2/H+-induced vasodilation were to occur in chemosensitive regions it would accelerate removal of tissue CO2/H+ and effectively counter-regulate activity of respiratory chemoreceptors (Xie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2006.

claim: Fast breath by breath changes in arteriole CO2 correspond with changes in pH measured at the ventral medullary surface.
source: Consistent with this, early studies showed that fast breath by breath changes in arteriole CO2 correspond with changes in pH measured at the ventral medullary surface (Millhorn et al., 1984), suggesting tissue pH in this region is not highly buffered, possibly because blood vessels in this region do not dilate in response to CO2/H+.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Millhorn et al., 1984.

claim: Tissue pH in the ventral medullary surface region is not highly buffered, possibly because blood vessels in this region do not dilate in response to CO2/H+.
source: Consistent with this, early studies showed that fast breath by breath changes in arteriole CO2 correspond with changes in pH measured at the ventral medullary surface (Millhorn et al., 1984), suggesting tissue pH in this region is not highly buffered, possibly because blood vessels in this region do not dilate in response to CO2/H+.
evidence: This is an inference based on data from Millhorn et al., 1984.

claim: CO2/H+-evoked ATP release appears to be a unique feature of RTN chemoreception.
source: Furthermore, considering that CO2/H+-evoked ATP release appears to be unique feature of RTN chemoreception (Gourine et al., 2010) and since ATP can mediate vasoconstriction in other brain regions (Kur and Newman, 2014; Peppiatt et al., 2006), we hypothesize that CO2/H+-evoked ATP release will antagonize CO2/H+-vasodilation in the RTN, and thus prevent CO2/H+ washout, further enhancing chemoreceptor function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gourine et al., 2010.

claim: ATP can mediate vasoconstriction in other brain regions.
source: Furthermore, considering that CO2/H+-evoked ATP release appears to be unique feature of RTN chemoreception (Gourine et al., 2010) and since ATP can mediate vasoconstriction in other brain regions (Kur and Newman, 2014; Peppiatt et al., 2006), we hypothesize that CO2/H+-evoked ATP release will antagonize CO2/H+-vasodilation in the RTN, and thus prevent CO2/H+ washout, further enhancing chemoreceptor function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kur and Newman, 2014 and Peppiatt et al., 2006.

claim: Exposure to CO2/H+ caused vasoconstriction of RTN arterioles in vitro.
source: For example, exposure to CO2/H+ under control conditions resulted in a vasoconstriction of −4.6 ± 0.6% (p<0.0001, N = 34 vessels) (Figure 1C) (estimated by Poiseuille's law to decrease blood flow by ~20%).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles is estimated by Poiseuille's law to decrease blood flow by ~20%.
source: For example, exposure to CO2/H+ under control conditions resulted in a vasoconstriction of −4.6 ± 0.6% (p<0.0001, N = 34 vessels) (Figure 1C) (estimated by Poiseuille's law to decrease blood flow by ~20%).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data using Poiseuille's law.

claim: CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles was retained in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX) to block neuronal action potentials.
source: Further, we found that CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles was retained in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX; 0.5 µM) to block neuronal action potentials (−6.1 ± 1.6%, p=0.0103, N = 6 vessels), thus suggesting glutamatergic CO2/H+-activated neurons (Mulkey et al., 2004) are not requisite determinants of this response.
evidence: This is an experimental finding that supports the claim that neurons are not required for the vascular response.

claim: Glutamatergic CO2/H+-activated neurons are not requisite determinants of CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles.
source: Further, we found that CO2/H+-induced constriction of RTN arterioles was retained in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX; 0.5 µM) to block neuronal action potentials (−6.1 ± 1.6%, p=0.0103, N = 6 vessels), thus suggesting glutamatergic CO2/H+-activated neurons (Mulkey et al., 2004) are not requisite determinants of this response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TTX experiment and supported by citation to Mulkey et al., 2004.

claim: Exposure to CO2/H+ did not cause constriction of RTN arterioles during P2 receptor blockade with 5 µM PPADS.
source: Conversely, exposure to CO2/H+ did not cause constriction of RTN arterioles during P2 receptor blockade with 5 µM PPADS (−0.1 ± 0.9%, p=0.4876, N = 8 vessels) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Exposure to ATP (100 µM) resulted in constriction of RTN arterioles.
source: Indeed, we found that exposure to ATP (100 µM) resulted in a −5.8 ± 1.5% constriction (p=0.0018, N = 7 vessels) (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Purinergic signaling contributes to CO2/H+-dependent control of RTN arterioles.
source: These results show that purinergic signaling contributes to CO2/H+-dependent control of RTN arterioles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing effects of PPADS and ATP.

claim: PPADS at 5 µM has highest affinities for P2X and P2Y2 and P2Y4 receptors.
source: Since the concentration of PPADS used above to block purinergic modulation of RTN arterioles has highest affinities for P2X and P2Y2 and P2Y4 (Ralevic and Burnstock, 1998), to identify candidate P2 receptors that help maintain RTN arteriole tone during exposure to CO2/H+, we tested effects of a selective P2Y2 and P2Y4 receptor agonist (UTPγS) (Lazarowski et al., 1996) and an agonist with high affinity for P2X receptors (α,β-mATP) (Burnstock and Kennedy, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ralevic and Burnstock, 1998.

claim: Bath application of UTPγS (0.5 µM) decreased diameter of RTN arterioles.
source: We found that bath application of UTPγS (0.5 µM) mimicked effects of CO2/H+ by decreasing diameter of RTN arterioles (−3.4 ± 0.6%, p=0.0003, N = 8 vessels), whereas exposure to α,β-mATP (100 µM) minimally affected arteriole tone (p=0.2113, N = 9 vessels) (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Exposure to α,β-mATP (100 µM) minimally affected RTN arteriole tone.
source: We found that bath application of UTPγS (0.5 µM) mimicked effects of CO2/H+ by decreasing diameter of RTN arterioles (−3.4 ± 0.6%, p=0.0003, N = 8 vessels), whereas exposure to α,β-mATP (100 µM) minimally affected arteriole tone (p=0.2113, N = 9 vessels) (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Mechanisms underlying purinergic-dependent control of RTN arterioles during high CO2/H+ involve activation of Gq-coupled P2Y2/4 receptors.
source: These results suggest that mechanism(s) underlying purinergic-dependent control of RTN arterioles during high CO2/H+ involve activation of Gq-coupled P2Y2/4 receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of UTPγS and α,β-mATP.

claim: P2Y2 and P2Y4 immunoreactivity was detected in close proximity to endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, and astrocytes associated with RTN arterioles.
source: We detected P2Y2 and P2Y4 immunoreactivity in close proximity to all three cell types associated with RTN arterioles. For example, P2Y2 and P2Y4 labeling appeared as numerous intensely stained puncta near endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells and as smaller more diffuse puncta near astrocytes (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: P2Y2/4 receptors contribute to purinergic-dependent vasoconstriction in the RTN during exposure to CO2/H+.
source: The expression of these receptors together with our functional evidence suggest P2Y2/4 receptors contribute to purinergic-dependent vasoconstriction in the RTN during exposure to CO2/H+.
evidence: This is an inference based on immunohistochemistry and functional data.

claim: Application of adenosine (1 µM) caused vasodilation of RTN arterioles.
source: We found that application of adenosine (1 µM) under control conditions caused vasodilation of RTN arterioles (2.6 ± 0.6%; p=0.0027, N = 9 vessels) (Figure 1D–E);
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Blockade of adenosine receptors with 8-phenyltheophylline (8-PT; 10 µM) had negligible effects on CO2/H+-induced vasoconstriction of RTN arterioles.
source: however, blockade of adenosine receptors with 8-phenyltheophylline (8-PT; 10 µM) had negligible effects on CO2/H+-induced vasoconstriction (−3.2 ± 0.4%, p=0.0002, N = 7 vessels) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Incubation in sodium metatungstate (POM 1; 100 µM) to inhibit ectonucleotidase activity minimally affected the CO2/H+-vascular response of RTN arterioles.
source: Likewise, incubation in sodium metatungstate (POM 1; 100 µM) to inhibit ectonucleotidase activity also minimally affected the CO2/H+-vascular response of RTN arterioles (−3.1 ± 0.6%, p=0.0195, N = 5 vessels) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Nucleoside metabolites are not essential for CO2/H+-dependent regulation of vascular tone in the RTN.
source: These results suggest that nucleoside metabolites are not essential for CO2/H+-dependent regulation of vascular tone in the RTN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of P1 receptor blockade and ectonucleotidase inhibition.

claim: CO2/H+-evoked ATP release from RTN astrocytes is mediated by intracellular Ca2+.
source: Previous evidence (Gourine et al., 2010) suggests CO2/H+-evoked ATP release from RTN astrocytes is mediated by intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gourine et al., 2010.

claim: Exposure to t-ACPD caused vasoconstriction of RTN arterioles under baseline conditions but not in PPADS.
source: Exposure to t-ACPD caused vasoconstriction of RTN arterioles under baseline conditions (−3.5 ± 0.5%, p=0.0007, N = 7) but not in PPADS (−0.6 ± 0.4%, p=0.2163, N = 7 vessels) (Figure 2A–B,E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2A-B,E.

claim: Purinergic signaling, possibly from CO2/H+-sensitive RTN astrocytes, serves to maintain tone of arterioles in the RTN during hypercapnia.
source: These results are consistent with our hypothesis that purinergic signaling, possibly from CO2/H+-sensitive RTN astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010), serves to maintain tone of arteriole in the RTN during hypercapnia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the t-ACPD experiments and supported by citation to Gourine et al., 2010.

claim: Bath application of t-ACPD (50 µM) dilated cortical arterioles.
source: In marked contrast to the RTN, we found that cortical arterioles dilated in response to astrocyte activation by t-ACPD. For example, bath application of t-ACPD (50 µM) dilated cortical arterioles by 3.2 ± 0.6% (p=0.0030, N = 5 vessels) (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The t-ACPD response of cortical arterioles is consistent with previous cortical studies.
source: This response is consistent with previous cortical studies (Filosa et al., 2004; Zonta et al., 2003), and suggests that astrocytes in the RTN and cortex have fundamentally different roles in regulation of vascular tone.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filosa et al., 2004 and Zonta et al., 2003.

claim: Astrocytes in the RTN and cortex have fundamentally different roles in regulation of vascular tone.
source: This response is consistent with previous cortical studies (Filosa et al., 2004; Zonta et al., 2003), and suggests that astrocytes in the RTN and cortex have fundamentally different roles in regulation of vascular tone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential responses to t-ACPD in RTN vs cortex.

claim: Cortical arterioles dilate in response to CO2/H+.
source: Also consistent with previous work (Ainslie and Duffin, 2009), we confirmed that cortical arterioles dilate in response to CO2/H+(5.7 ± 1.1%, p=0.0057, N = 11 vessels) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3A-C and consistent with cited literature.

claim: The CO2/H+-vascular response of cortical arterioles was reduced in PPADS.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the CO2/H+-vascular response of cortical arterioles was reduced to 0.5 ± 0.5% in PPADS (p=0.004, N = 6 vessels) (Figure 3A–C), suggesting involvement of endogenous ATP in cortical arteriole CO2/H+-dilation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Endogenous ATP is involved in cortical arteriole CO2/H+-dilation.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the CO2/H+-vascular response of cortical arterioles was reduced to 0.5 ± 0.5% in PPADS (p=0.004, N = 6 vessels) (Figure 3A–C), suggesting involvement of endogenous ATP in cortical arteriole CO2/H+-dilation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of PPADS on cortical arteriole CO2/H+ response.

claim: Endothelial cells, smooth muscle and astrocytes associated with cortical arterioles were immunoreactive for P2Y2 and P2Y4.
source: As in the RTN, we also found that endothelial cells, smooth muscle and astrocytes associated with cortical arterioles were immunoreactive for P2Y2 and P2Y4 (Figure 3D–E), suggesting the differential roles of purinergic signaling in these regions is not due to the presence or absence of P2Y2 and P2Y4.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The differential roles of purinergic signaling in the RTN and cortex is not due to the presence or absence of P2Y2 and P2Y4.
source: As in the RTN, we also found that endothelial cells, smooth muscle and astrocytes associated with cortical arterioles were immunoreactive for P2Y2 and P2Y4 (Figure 3D–E), suggesting the differential roles of purinergic signaling in these regions is not due to the presence or absence of P2Y2 and P2Y4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data showing similar receptor expression in both regions.

claim: In vivo application of a selective P2Y1 receptor blocker (MRS2179, 100 µM) had no measurable effect on the CO2/H+ response of pial vessels in the RTN.
source: However, we found that in vivo application of a selective P2Y1 receptor blocker (MRS2179, 100 µM) had no measurable effect on the CO2/H+ response of pial vessels in the RTN (−3.7 ± 0.8%, vs. saline plus CO2: −4.3 ± 0.7%; p=0.068; N = 5 vessels) or cortex (4.8 ± 0.5%, vs. saline plus CO2: 4.7 ± 0.6%; p=0.24; N = 5 vessels) (data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: In vivo application of a selective P2Y1 receptor blocker (MRS2179, 100 µM) had no measurable effect on the CO2/H+ response of pial vessels in the cortex.
source: However, we found that in vivo application of a selective P2Y1 receptor blocker (MRS2179, 100 µM) had no measurable effect on the CO2/H+ response of pial vessels in the RTN (−3.7 ± 0.8%, vs. saline plus CO2: −4.3 ± 0.7%; p=0.068; N = 5 vessels) or cortex (4.8 ± 0.5%, vs. saline plus CO2: 4.7 ± 0.6%; p=0.24; N = 5 vessels) (data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: CO2/H+-mediated vasodilation in the cortex and hippocampus involved activation of cyclooxygenase-1 and prostaglandin E2 release by astrocytes.
source: Alternatively, arachidonic acid metabolites are also potent regulators of vascular tone (MacVicar and Newman, 2015) and recent evidence showed that CO2/H+-mediated vasodilation in the cortex and hippocampus involved activation of cyclooxygenase-1 and prostaglandin E2 release by astrocytes (Howarth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacVicar and Newman, 2015 and Howarth et al., 2017.

claim: Purinergic signaling can elicit Ca2+ responses in astrocytes to facilitate prostaglandin E2 synthesis.
source: Considering that purinergic signaling can elicit Ca2+ responses in astrocytes to facilitate prostaglandin E2 synthesis (Xu et al., 2003), it remains possible that purinergic signaling contributes to cortical CO2/H+ dilation by influencing synthesis and release of prostaglandin E2 by astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2003 and is presented as speculation.

claim: Localized application of the vasoconstrictor phenylephrine (1 µM) to the ventral medullary surface enhanced the ventilatory response to CO2 by increasing diaphragm EMG amplitude by 15 ± 2%.
source: We found that localized application of the vasoconstrictors phenylephrine (Phe; 1 µM) or U46619 (1 µM) to the ventral medullary surface (VMS) enhanced the ventilatory response to CO2 by increasing diaphragm electromyogram (EMG) amplitude 15 ± 2% and 18 ± 1.8%, respectively (Figure 4A–C) (p=0.02; N = 6 animals) but with no change in frequency (Figure 4D) (p>0.05; N = 6 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Localized application of the vasoconstrictor U46619 (1 µM) to the ventral medullary surface enhanced the ventilatory response to CO2 by increasing diaphragm EMG amplitude by 18 ± 1.8%.
source: We found that localized application of the vasoconstrictors phenylephrine (Phe; 1 µM) or U46619 (1 µM) to the ventral medullary surface (VMS) enhanced the ventilatory response to CO2 by increasing diaphragm electromyogram (EMG) amplitude 15 ± 2% and 18 ± 1.8%, respectively (Figure 4A–C) (p=0.02; N = 6 animals) but with no change in frequency (Figure 4D) (p>0.05; N = 6 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: VMS application of the vasodilator sodium nitroprusside (SNP; 1 µM) decreased ventilatory response to CO2 by decreasing diaphragm amplitude by 24 ± 2.6%.
source: Also consistent with the possibility that increased blood flow will facilitate removal of tissue CO2/H+, and thus decrease the stimulus to chemosensitive neurons, we found that VMS application of the vasodilator sodium nitroprusside (SNP; 1 µM) decreased ventilatory response to CO2 by decreasing diaphragm amplitude by 24 ± 2.6% (Figure 4A–C) (p=0.02; N = 6 animals) but with no change in frequency (Figure 4D) (p>0.05; N = 6 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: VMS application of phenylephrine, SNP, or U46619 had negligible effect on systemic mean arterial pressure (MAP).
source: These treatments had negligible effect on systemic mean arterial pressure (MAP) (Phe: 110 ± 2; SNP: 110 ± 2; U4619: 108 ± 3 vs. saline: 109 ± 2 mmHg; p>0.05) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: Regulation of vascular tone in the RTN can influence respiratory output.
source: These results are consistent with the possibility that regulation of vascular tone in the RTN can influence respiratory output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of vasoconstrictors and vasodilators on respiratory output.

claim: Phenylephrine can directly stimulate activity of chemosensitive RTN neurons.
source: For example, phenylephrine can directly stimulate activity of chemosensitive RTN neurons (Kuo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuo et al., 2016.

claim: Effects of phenylephrine on chemoreception likely involves both vasoconstriction and direct neural activation.
source: Therefore, effects of phenylephrine on chemoreception likely involves both vasoconstriction and direct neural activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known effects of phenylephrine on both vessels and neurons.

claim: Increasing end-expiratory CO2 to 9.5–10% constricted VMS vessels by −4.5 ± 0.5% in vivo.
source: Consistent with our in vitro data, we found that increasing end-expiratory CO2 to 9.5–10%, which corresponds with an arterial pH of 7.2 pH units (Guyenet et al., 2005), constricted VMS vessels by −4.5 ± 0.5% (p=0.014, N = 5 animals) (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5A-B and consistent with cited literature.

claim: When P2-receptors are blocked with PPADS (10 µM), increasing inspired CO2 resulted in a vasodilation of 4.3 ± 0.4% in VMS vessels.
source: However, when P2-receptors are blocked with PPADS (10 µM), increasing inspired CO2 resulted in a vasodilation of 4.3 ± 0.4% (Figure 5A–B) (p=0.036; N = 5 animals).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: In the RTN, purinergic-mediated vasoconstriction is working against a background CO2/H+ dilation, possibly mediated by a cyclooxygenase/prostaglandin E2-dependent mechanism.
source: This suggests that in the RTN, purinergic-mediated vasoconstriction is working against a background CO2/H+ dilation, possibly mediated by a cyclooxygenenase/prostroglandine E2-dependent mechanism as described elsewhere in the brain (Howarth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the PPADS experiment and supported by citation to Howarth et al., 2017.

claim: Administration of a cyclooxygenase inhibitor (indomethacin) has been shown to increase baseline breathing and the ventilatory response to CO2 in humans.
source: Consistent with this, administration of a cyclooxygenase inhibitor (indomethacin) has been shown to increase baseline breathing and the ventilatory response to CO2 in humans (Xie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2006.

claim: Global disruption of cerebrovascular CO2/H+ reactivity is associated with certain pathological states including heart failure and stroke.
source: It should also be noted that global disruption of cerebrovascular CO2/H+ reactivity as associated with certain pathological states including heart failure and stroke (Yonas et al., 1993; Howard et al., 2001) or by systemic administration of indomethacin can increase chemoreceptor gain to the extent that breathing becomes unstable (Fan et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yonas et al., 1993 and Howard et al., 2001.

claim: Global disruption of cerebrovascular CO2/H+ reactivity by systemic administration of indomethacin can increase chemoreceptor gain to the extent that breathing becomes unstable.
source: It should also be noted that global disruption of cerebrovascular CO2/H+ reactivity as associated with certain pathological states including heart failure and stroke (Yonas et al., 1993; Howard et al., 2001) or by systemic administration of indomethacin can increase chemoreceptor gain to the extent that breathing becomes unstable (Fan et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fan et al., 2010 and Xie et al., 2009.

claim: Exogenous application of ATP (1 mM) constricted VMS vessels by −5.1 ± 0.6% in vivo.
source: Also consistent with our slice data, we found that exogenous application of ATP (1 mM) or UTPγS (1 mM) constricted VMS vessels by −5.1 ± 0.6% and −5.0 ± 0.5%, respectively (p=0.001; N = 5 animals) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Exogenous application of UTPγS (1 mM) constricted VMS vessels by −5.0 ± 0.5% in vivo.
source: Also consistent with our slice data, we found that exogenous application of ATP (1 mM) or UTPγS (1 mM) constricted VMS vessels by −5.1 ± 0.6% and −5.0 ± 0.5%, respectively (p=0.001; N = 5 animals) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Cortical pial vessels dilated in response to an increase in inspired CO2 under control conditions (5 ± 0.5%) in vivo.
source: Conversely, cortical pial vessels dilated in response to an increase in inspired CO2 under control conditions (5 ± 0.5%) and after application of 10 µM PPADS (3.2 ± 0.3%) (Figure 5C) (p=0.03; N = 5 animals);
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The CO2/H+-induced vasodilation of cortical vessels was blunted in the presence of PPADS in vivo.
